session_title: Report on the 'Excavation' of Old Objects

content.text: Shuying, while tidying up the old house in the countryside recently, I came across this old item. Looking at it, I feel as though I can touch the traces of time. It has been almost two months since we last planned to make Qingtuan together—time really flies.

Huai'an, the details of this lock are truly exquisite! The color scheme of the embroidery reminds me of a description from a certain novel, evoking a sense of quietness intertwined with stories. Does it carry any memories? This reminds me of when we first talked about Qingtuan, and you mentioned that 'rustic charm of handmade crafts.' Every old object is like a slice of time.

Yes, this was a gift from the master to my grandfather when he left after working for a wealthy family back in the day. It had been hidden in a corner of the old house until now, finally seeing the light of day again. It reminds me of those old photos of Qingtuan I shared last time—they, too, are memories preserved in this way.

I see. Does this lock have any special meaning? I always feel that behind old objects, there are hidden depths, much like the regional charm in the rustic craftsmanship we discussed earlier when talking about Qingtuan. Do you remember the chart you shared about the differences in Qingtuan across the Jiangnan region? That meticulous attention to detail is quite similar to interpreting the story behind this lock.

The meaning is about protection and inheritance. Grandpa said that the owner gave this lock in the hope that it would secure the craftsmanship and memories, passing them down through generations. This reminds me of the value of handmade work you emphasized when we made Qingtuan together. That time, we divided the tasks—you were in charge of the savory filling, and I handled the sweet filling—wasn’t it also about preserving and presenting different "individual narratives"?

Huai'an, I just found similar descriptions in some books that closely resemble those in this one. Look, here it mentions that copper locks in the late Qing Dynasty often symbolize family harmony, which aligns well with what you said about protection. It's like the green rice cake-making flowchart I found last time, which preserves wisdom and steps in a paper-based format.

Thank you for sharing. The details on these book pages have further convinced me of their age. The patterns on the lock body might also reflect the aesthetic preferences of affluent families at the time, much like your previous recommendation of 'Gumaimeng' rice flour, which showcased a meticulous choice in product packaging and quality. Our examination of "objects" always unconsciously carries a quest for beauty and history.

Yes, personal narratives always shine through these old objects. Do you think this item should be restored, preserved as is, or 're-presented' in some form? Just like when we discussed qingtuan, balancing tradition and innovation—should we strictly follow the old recipe, or make personalized adjustments to the sweet and savory fillings as we planned?

I prefer to preserve the original state, allowing rust and wear to remain as part of its history. Restoration might strip away that authentic touch, much like the rustic charm of qingtuan in old photographs—its simplicity is its soul. Remember when we talked about "slow living"? Perhaps preserving without intervention is itself a form of respect for the traces of time.

I understand your thoughts, but perhaps a gentle cleaning could make the patterns clearer while preserving the traces of time. This reminds me of your meticulousness when consulting the elderly for traditional Qingtuan recipes—always seeking continuity through preservation. Just like how you referred to that detailed guide for making Qingtuan dough, you honor tradition while making the process clearer and more feasible.

Here's another close-up of the lock's keyhole. The structure of the keyhole reminds me of the breathability of bamboo steamers—both are examples of wisdom embedded in old objects. In the photos you shared last time, the glutinous rice balls steamed in that bamboo steamer had such a delightfully chewy texture. This ancient design wisdom, much like the mechanical structure of this lock, is truly worth savoring.

Yes, this kind of wisdom deserves to be represented again. Perhaps we can write a short story for it, combining Grandpa's memories, just as you connected the past with old photos before, bringing tangible memories to life. This aligns seamlessly with our plan to explore the flavors of Qingtuan and document the making process—both are about building a 'personal memory archive.'

Great idea, this lock can become part of our cultural roots exploration. From green rice balls to bronze locks, each discovery deepens our understanding of slow living. Would you like to help organize these narratives together? Just as we agreed to exchange green rice balls and share stories offline, let this discovery also become part of our collective action.

Of course, I'd love to! This reminds me of the anticipation we felt when planning to exchange green rice cakes offline, and now there's an added joy of sharing discoveries. The warmth of paper and the continuity of history converge here. Remember how we talked about meeting at my bookstore? The space, filled with stacks of old books, is perfect for taking a closer look at this lock and discussing the stories behind it.

Yes, this 'excavation' report has made me cherish these old objects even more. They are not just items; they are witnesses of time, much like the descriptions you found in books, adding layers to memory. It reminds me of our earlier conversation about Qingtuan—isn't that also adding a contemporary annotation to a fading 'regional essence'?

Huai'an, this conversation has truly been a profound 'reading' and 'interpretation.' From the symbolism of the lock to the methods of preservation, we have immersed ourselves in the joy of discovery, which carries more warmth than any mechanized production. Just as we resist the mechanized production of Qingtuan, our commitment to the value of craftsmanship and tangible memories remains the underlying tone of our dialogue.

Shuying, thank you for always resonating with these subtle details. Next time we meet, I can bring this lock to show you in person, just like how we shared the process of making Qingtuan before, to make the experience more complete. It's been a while since we last planned to meet, and reuniting with this "newly unearthed" old item will be quite meaningful.

Great! I'm looking forward to it. From the green rice balls of spring to the old copper locks, our conversations always find a balance between heritage and aesthetics, making me feel that slow living can truly be enriching. I'll prepare the tea and snacks, just as we agreed last time, to create an atmosphere perfect for savoring the 'aesthetics of life' slowly.

Yes, each exchange brings the past and present closer together. The discovery of this lock is like a new anchor, reminding us to safeguard these memories and continue our cultural journey. From 'evoking seasonal memories' to 'attempting handcrafts,' and now to 'new understandings of old objects,' this thread is becoming increasingly clear.

Huaian, let's call it a day for now. I've already started imagining the story for this lock—it's sure to become a beautiful chapter in our shared narrative. Let's talk again later! Once we meet and exchange the green rice cakes, we'll take a good look at this lock together. It will be a perfect gathering of 'tangible memories.'
